analysis.one_liner: Lets each household exclude up to $10,000 of investment and pension income from federal income tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 1996 and never received a markup or vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have allowed every individual to leave up to $5,000 of unearned income off their taxable income each year — $10,000 for a married couple filing jointly [S2][S3]. "Unearned income" here means money not from a paycheck: dividends, interest, capital gains, rental income, and notably pension and annuity payments [S2][S3]. Someone whose income is entirely wages would get nothing, because wages and self-employment earnings are excluded from the break [S3]. The bill was introduced on March 7, 1996, sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, and never moved again before that Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households that already have investment or pension income: savers living off dividends, interest, capital gains, rental income, and retirees drawing pensions or annuities. A married couple with investment income could shelter an extra $10,000 a year from federal tax [S2][S3]. Because the exclusion is a flat dollar amount, it reaches middle-class pensioners, but the largest dollar benefit goes to those with the most investment income to shield — and it does nothing for anyone whose income comes only from work [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with investment and pension income

how_it_helps.text: Each individual could exclude up to $5,000 of unearned income ($10,000 on a joint return) from gross income each year, cutting their federal income tax [S2][S3].
The exclusion covers pension and annuity income, so retirees drawing a pension would pay tax on less of it [S2][S3].
It applied to income beginning in the first tax year after enactment, with no phase-out based on how much money a household has [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dollar excluded is a dollar not collected in tax, so the cost shows up as higher deficits or higher taxes elsewhere. And because the benefit is only available on unearned income, households living entirely on wages effectively shoulder a relatively larger share of the remaining tax burden [S3].

drawbacks.text: The break reaches only people who already have investment or pension income; a worker whose entire income is wages, salary, or tips cannot use it at all, so it tilts the tax code toward wealth over work [S3].

A flat exclusion gives the same dollar benefit to a wealthy investor and a modest pensioner, meaning the richest households keep the largest amounts of untaxed money and the government collects less overall, which must be made up through borrowing or other taxes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a retiree or a middle-income household with a small pension, an extra $5,000-$10,000 sheltered from tax is real money. But the design is bottom-heavy in the wrong way: the benefit is unavailable to wage earners and, because it is not means-tested, the largest tax savings go to households with the most investment income. A credit or an exclusion capped per person regardless of income type would deliver relief to working and retired households more evenly; as written, this mainly trims taxes on capital.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Cleo Fields, a Democrat from Louisiana, introduced the Tax-Free Savings and Investment Income Act on March 7, 1996 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel that writes tax law, on the day it was introduced [S5].
That was the last action ever taken: the committee never considered it, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill died with no vote in either chamber [S5].
It had only two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything, because the bill died without action. Had it passed, households with investment and pension income would have paid less tax, paid for by other taxpayers or higher deficits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill died in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls reveal where parties stood; its sponsor was a Democrat and its two cosponsors split one Democrat and one Republican [S4].

industries.note: Investors with dividend, interest, capital gain, and rental income could each shield up to $5,000-$10,000 a year from tax, and funds that market such income would have a more attractive product to sell. The cost lands on the Treasury and, relative to a wage-only earner, on households whose income comes from work [S3].

Because the exclusion has no income limit, the households with the most investment income would keep the largest untaxed amounts, while the revenue gap would be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing [S3].
Pension and annuity income counts as unearned income under the bill, so retirees would pay tax on less of it. This is the part of the bill that most directly reaches ordinary households [S2][S3].
